title: Explaining variation in mixed paternity across birds: a global comparative meta-analysis
text:
A global comparative phylogenetic meta-analysis of mixed-paternity prevalence across avian species.
375 species · 619 population estimates · 46,249 broods



This website presents the complete reproducible workflow for the flobal comparative meta-analysis of mixed-paternity prevalence across birds.






Core idea



Birds are central model systems for studying sexual selection and reproductive conflict, yet mixed-paternity prevalence is often comparatively low across species. This study aims to understand which ecological, social, and methodological factors explain variation in mixed paternity across birds.

3.3 Prepare data

3.3.1 Population identifier
Population identity was defined using study identity and rounded geographic coordinates, with latitude and longitude rounded to two decimal places prior to constructing the population identifier.


Code
mixed_pat <- mixed_pat_raw %>%
  mutate(
    Lat_round = round(Lat, 2),
    Long_round = round(Long, 2),
    population_id = paste(Study_ID, Lat_round, Long_round, sep = "_"),
    population_id = as.factor(population_id)
  )




3.3.2 Study and species formatting
The following step formats the main grouping variables used in the models and calculates the total number of broods by combining mixed- and non-mixed-brood counts.


Code
mixed_pat <- mixed_pat %>%
  mutate(
    Study_ID = as.factor(Study_ID),
    species_phylo_brms = as.factor(Clements_name),
    species_nonphylo = as.factor(Clements_name),

    n_mixed_broods = as.numeric(n_mixed_broods),
    n_non_mixed_broods = as.numeric(n_non_mixed_broods),
    n_total_broods = n_mixed_broods + n_non_mixed_broods
  )




3.3.3 Phylogeny preparation
Species names were harmonised between the mixed-paternity dataset and the phylogenetic tree prior to pruning the tree and generating the phylogenetic covariance matrix used in the Bayesian models.


Code
species_data <- mixed_pat %>%
  filter(!is.na(species_phylo_brms)) %>%
  pull(species_phylo_brms) %>%
  as.character() %>%
  unique()

species_tree <- tree$tip.label

species_for_tree <- intersect(species_data, species_tree)

tree_analysis <- ape::keep.tip(tree, species_for_tree)

phylo_mat <- ape::vcv.phylo(tree_analysis, corr = TRUE)

phylo_mat <- phylo_mat[
  sort(rownames(phylo_mat)),
  sort(colnames(phylo_mat))
]

mixed_pat <- mixed_pat %>%
  filter(species_phylo_brms %in% rownames(phylo_mat)) %>%
  mutate(
    species_phylo_brms = droplevels(species_phylo_brms),
    species_nonphylo = droplevels(species_nonphylo)
  )

title: 4  Overall model
text:
4.4 Modelling framework
Because brood-level paternity data are expected to exhibit substantial extra-binomial heterogeneity across references, populations, and species, we modelled mixed-paternity prevalence using beta-binomial generalised linear mixed-effects models with a logit link:
\[y_i \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}(n_i, \mu_i, \phi)\]
where \(y_i\) is the number of broods with mixed paternity, \(n_i\) is the total number of broods genotyped, \(\mu_i\) is the expected mixed-paternity prevalence, and the precision parameter \(\phi\) describes extra-binomial variation among study units.
The linear predictor was modelled as:
\[\mathrm{logit}(\mu_i) = \alpha + \mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta} + u_{\mathrm{reference}[i]} + u_{\mathrm{species}[i]} + u_{\mathrm{phylo}[i]}\]
where \(\alpha\) is the intercept, \(\mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}\) represents fixed biological and methodological moderators, and \(u_{\mathrm{reference}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{species}}\), and \(u_{\mathrm{phylo}}\) represent reference-level, non-phylogenetic species-level, and phylogenetically structured random effects, respectively.

title: 4  Overall model
text:
4.5 Overall mixed-paternity prevalence

4.5.1 Model
The intercept-only model estimated the average mixed-paternity prevalence across studies and species while accounting for study-level, non-phylogenetic species-level, and phylogenetically structured species-level variation.


Code
model_overall_study <- brm(
  n_mixed_broods | trials(n_total_broods) ~
    1 +
    (1 | Study_ID) +
    (1 | species_nonphylo) +
    (1 | gr(species_phylo_brms, cov = phylo_mat)),
  family = beta_binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = data_overall_study,
  data2 = list(phylo_mat = phylo_mat),
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  iter = 10000,
  warmup = 5000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 15),
  seed = 123
)

4.5.5 Phylogenetic signal
We quantified the phylogenetic signal in between-species variation as the proportion of species-level variance attributable to the phylogenetically structured random effect:
\[
\nu =
\frac{\sigma^2_{\mathrm{phylo}}}
{\sigma^2_{\mathrm{phylo}} + \sigma^2_{\mathrm{nonphylo}}}
\]
where \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{phylo}}\) is the variance of the phylogenetically structured species-level random effect and \(\sigma^2_{\mathrm{nonphylo}}\) is the variance of the non-phylogenetic species-level random effect.

6.4 Model
This helper function documents the shared model structure used for all single-moderator models. These models are fitted outside this website workflow and saved as .rds files.


Code
fit_single_moderator <- function(formula, data) {
  brm(
    formula = formula,
    data = data,
    family = beta_binomial(link = "logit"),
    data2 = list(phylo_mat = phylo_mat),
    chains = 4,
    cores = 4,
    iter = 10000,
    warmup = 5000,
    control = list(
      adapt_delta = 0.99,
      max_treedepth = 15
    ),
    seed = 123
  )
}

title: 7  Biological moderators

7.3 Model
This helper function documents the shared model structure used for all single-moderator models. These models are fitted outside this website workflow and saved as .rds files.


Code
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

fit_single_moderator <- function(formula, data) {
  brm(
    formula = formula,
    data = data,
    family = beta_binomial(link = "logit"),
    data2 = list(phylo_mat = phylo_mat),
    chains = 4,
    cores = 4,
    iter = 10000,
    warmup = 5000,
    control = list(
      adapt_delta = 0.99,
      max_treedepth = 15
    ),
    seed = 123
  )
}

7.4 Nest type architecture
This model tested whether mixed-paternity prevalence differed among nest-type categories. Nest type was derived from BIRDBASE and simplified into four broad nest-architecture categories: cavity, ground, open, and other enclosed nests. Cavity nests included tree cavities and crevices; ground nests included burrows, scrapes, mounds, and nests placed directly on or in the ground; open nests included cups, saucers, platforms, and half-cups; and other enclosed nests included domes, pendant and globular nests, as well as nests built in other birds’ nests.

    plot_data[[cat_var]] <- factor(plot_data[[cat_var]], levels = names(labels), labels = labels)
  }
  
  ggplot() +
    geom_jitter(
      data = plot_data,
      aes(x = .data[[cat_var]], y = observed_prev, size = n_total_broods),
      width = 0.12,
      alpha = 0.25,
      colour = "#F4A261"
    ) +
    geom_pointrange(

    ) +

    ) +
